item.title: APO-DD: Dialogue Disentanglement via Reflective Optimization of Multi-Component Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2606.07894v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In multi-party chat, interleaved dialogues make it difficult to identify the context of each utterance. Dialogue disentanglement separates these dialogues to support dialogue analysis and response generation. Prompt refinement can improve large language models' (LLMs') accuracy on this task, but manually finding effective prompts for each LLM requires extensive trial and error. We propose APO-DD, which adapts GEPA to optimize prompts using execution traces and reflections on failed decisions. It updates task instructions directly and chat representations through automatically generated formatting functions. We compare optimizing either component alone or both. With Qwen3.5-9B, the best optimized prompt achieves an average score of 68.7 across seven evaluation metrics on Ubuntu IRC, compared with 57.5 for the best manually refined prompt. It also outperforms manually refined prompts on other chat domains without further optimization. For this model, optimizing task instructions alone does not always improve accuracy over the initial prompts. Our results suggest that exploring chat representation as an optimization target may yield higher accuracy than optimizing task instructions alone. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DB6B.
item.dc:creator: Naoki Takada, Tomohiro Okatsu, Yin Min Pa Pa, Katsunari Yoshioka, Tatsunori Mori

item.title: A Multi-Dimensional, Per-Pass Empirical Study of the LLVM Optimization Pipeline
item.description: arXiv:2606.31238v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantifying the marginal impact of individual optimization passes underpins phase ordering, pass selection, optimization design, and analysis of pass/hardware interactions. In LLVM, the standard backend for C/C++, Rust, and ML stacks via MLIR, interactions among passes, measurement noise, and pipeline scale make this difficult. We present a systematic empirical study of the LLVM -O3 pipeline. We decompose it into 113 cumulative per-pass prefixes and measure execution time, compile time, binary size, hardware counters, and RAPL energy on 30 PolyBench/C kernels (84,750 measurements). Transitions whose binary is byte-identical to their predecessor give us a built-in null distribution, which we use to calibrate every significance claim. On these compute-bound affine kernels, the pipeline is non-monotone: 36% of the transitions that significantly change runtime are regressions, found in 28 of 30 kernels. Gains are back-loaded (the median kernel needs 84.8% of the pipeline for 80% of its speedup) and concentrated in a small core of passes, a result that holds under both absolute and scale-free impact measures. IR instruction count is an unreliable runtime predictor, and runtime-targeted passes are de facto energy-targeted (30-60% savings). Finally, we bound the speedup lost to non-monotone behavior from above by 46.35% and decompose it: 9.7 points are measurement noise, 15.3 points are transient dips repaired within three passes, and only 21.3 points persist to the end of the pipeline. These findings inform pass pruning, cost-model calibration, and autotuning.
item.dc:creator: Federico Bruzzone, Walter Cazzola

item.title: No Edges, No Verdict: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Declared Dependency Graphs in 78K SBOMs in the Wild
item.description: arXiv:2607.22140v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) are consumed not only as component inventories but as dependency graphs: vulnerability triage, reachability filtering, and impact analysis all traverse the edges an SBOM declares. We present the first large-scale characterization of the declared dependency graph across 78,612 real-world SBOM files from the Wild SBOMs dataset (77,092 parseable). We find that the population splits into three regimes: 52.9% of SBOMs declare no edges at all (failing the NTIA minimum-elements requirement of dependency relationships; 42.3% once the 46.5% of files carrying the tool entry of a single generation harness are set aside), 8.8% declare a dependency block yet leave the majority of components isolated (degenerate regime; among such SBOMs with at least 50 components the median orphan share is 93%, and our 11 Syft-generated container-image SBOMs fall in this regime at 91.4-98.0% orphans), and 38.3% form well-connected graphs. Edge emission is predicted by the generator rather than by the format (0%-100% no-edge rates across tools), and the specification-level mechanism for declaring graph incompleteness (CycloneDX compositions) is used by 0.10% of CycloneDX documents. We argue that in the first two regimes, the common consumer inference "no path implies unreachable" is an unsound closed-world conclusion drawn from a demonstrably incomplete artifact; in a production vulnerability-prioritization system, replacing the resulting veto with an explicit "unknown" level guarded by a degeneracy detector recovered KEV recall from 0.600 to 0.950 (controlled re-scoring; 0.957 in a live end-to-end run) without alert flooding. The streaming scanner and the full per-SBOM topology dataset are archived on Zenodo.

item.title: AuditCoder: Process-Auditable Code Generation through Responsibility-Preserving Task Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2607.29529v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Plans can guide code generation without record?ing which code implements each subproblem, leaving reviewers to reconstruct these links dur?ing handoff and maintenance. We present AU?DITCODER, a multi-agent system for process?auditable code generation that jointly con?structs a program and its responsibility record. A contract-annotated task graph assigns sta?ble IDs before implementation and preserves code ownership through generation and assem?bly. The same IDs connect each planning commitment to its code, versioned check results, and repair history, supporting human inspec?tion and automated checks of record complete?ness and repair decisions. When failure evidence supports a node or branch, bounded repair declares an editable scope, records any expansion, and leaves code outside the final scope unchanged. The system abstains when no boundary is supported. On a 200-task APPS sample and ClassEval, AUDITCODER remains competitive with CodeSim across two models under a one-round feedback limit. The DeepSeek-based system also remains compet?itive on 22 exploratory cross-domain tasks. An audit of the DeepSeek APPS run finds that, averaged across tasks, 97.25% of final leaf records retain nonempty code, contract, provenance, and check fields. All 44 repair attempts follow the recorded accept/rollback policy, and 30 pass held-out tests, with scopes averaging 22% of graph nodes. Anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuditCoder/.
item.dc:creator: Kangjie Huang, Hui Zhou, Chen Lyu

item.title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
item.description: arXiv:2610.30016v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.
item.dc:creator: Sujoy Roychowdhury, Joseph H. R. Isaac, Jiangning Gao, Martin Klitte, Diarmuid Corcoran

item.title: PosterHarness: Turning Scientific Poster Generation into an Auditable Instruction-Following Benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2607.03006v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-rich image models can now design poster-scale layouts, but we lack ways to measure whether they honor scientific communication contracts: legible labels, prescribed aspect ratios, and -- above all -- abstaining from fabricated scientific figures. We present POSTERHARNESS, an auditable harness reframing poster generation as measurable instruction-following tasks, with a pilot benchmark and failure taxonomy. POSTERHARNESS uses a placeholder-first contract to separate two jobs models otherwise conflate. The model performs visual-summary design: typography, reading path, color, and background -- but never draws data-bearing figures. Every figure region must be an empty labeled placeholder; a deterministic compositor inserts real source-paper figures at detected coordinates. This makes properties measurable: placeholder count and ID accuracy, blankness, aspect-ratio compliance, abstention from synthesized graphics, public-text hygiene, and source-figure provenance -- with failures logged as explicit rejections, not hidden in plausible-looking output. We instantiate the harness on 12 papers (6 HEP, 6 AI/ML-adjacent) and report three findings. (i) A counterfactual probe shows the placeholder contract drives VLM-counted synthesized figures from 34 to 0 across three papers. (ii) A failure taxonomy identifies blocking contracts: placeholder geometry, placeholder QA, template critic, and public text. (iii) Comparison with Paper2Poster shows a trade-off: PosterHarness yields higher-resolution artifacts, lower white-canvas fraction, and stronger VLM visual preference; the deterministic baseline retains slightly more PosterQuiz-style information and runs faster. We report this as regime characterization, not a superiority claim. All artifacts, prompts, manifests, and audit scripts are released as a reusable evaluation component.
item.dc:creator: Tianyi Yang, Dawei Fu, Youpeng Wu, Zixun Kou, Linrui Chen, Ruobing Jiang, Zijian Wang, Qiang Li

item.title: Extending FunctionGemma for Practical On-Device Mobile Function Calling
item.description: arXiv:2609.25373v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-device assistants require function-calling models that map natural language to local system actions, but existing resources emphasize web APIs or narrow mobile-action catalogs. We extend FunctionGemma 270M-it to practical Android workflows by introducing MOBILEACTIONSEXTENDED, a synthetic, schema-validated dataset of ~9,500 conversations covering fifteen device-control categories, including messaging, phone calls, camera/screenshot, brightness control, device-status queries, flashlight control, and application management. We fine-tune the 270M model with TRL supervised fine-tuning under completion-only loss, producing an extended specialist and a combined model trained jointly with Google's MOBILEACTIONSGOOGLE. On MOBILEACTIONSEXTENDED, end-to-end accuracy improves from 29.3% for the base model and 17.2% for Google's Mobile-Actions variant to 76.5%. The combined model retains 76.5% on MOBILEACTIONSEXTENDED and reaches 82.3% on MOBILEACTIONSGOOGLE, down from the 90.3% of Google's Mobile-Actions specialist, representing an 8.0-percentage-point trade-off in return for doubling category coverage. We release the dataset, fine-tuned models, reproducible training/evaluation pipeline, and an Android demo, highlighting compact local function calling as a practical path towards low-latency and privacy-preserving mobile assistants.
item.dc:creator: Ali Rezagholizadeh, Soheila Samiee

item.title: Operator Packages, Proposer Strength, and Construction-Family Plateaus in Office-Scale Verified Search
item.description: arXiv:2609.29636v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Verified search, in which a language model proposes programs, a hard evaluator scores them, and selection keeps the best, has recently moved mathematical records; controlled ablations of the proposer-side components remain rare. We instrument a minimal FunSearch-style loop at office scale (a 30B local model on a laptop, 120-600 verified samples per run) with three operator packages: a schematic notebook the model writes and carries instead of verbatim elites, a named obstacle, and behavioural repulsion from constructions already found. On nine construction problems from a public repository, the complete 2^3 factorial with two replicates favours the primary contrast in a nominal two-stage analysis: the composition closes more of the seed-to-record gap (+0.196; nominal pooled p=0.023, stage-combination p~0.08; median per-problem effect +0.045). Repulsion raises construction-hash diversity in eight of nine problems (one-sided p=0.0039; partly a manipulation check). The factorial finds no positive memory-by-repulsion interaction (bounded to about +/-0.04); the gain decomposes additively, and memory+repulsion is the only arm that never collapses (0 of 18 runs), within 0.025 of the full composition. A frontier proposer under the identical loop reaches in tens of samples what the local model does not in hundreds; in single scoping runs its gains arrive without the operators. The searches stall after closing 85-92% of the gap on the flagship problem, and a later analysis reads that plateau as a resolution limit: the reference value is a continuum limit and the unaided long-run finals already carry its family's structure. In the registered family-hint test the family named in words is adopted and loses; handed as code, it is optimized, but our best finite-grid encoding stays below the plateau reached unaided. We release the harness, every candidate, and the dated pre-registrations.
item.dc:creator: Roberto I. Ono Filho

item.title: Compositional Safety Failures in Harness Evolution: Identification and Runtime Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2609.33123v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Self-evolving agent harnesses continually update persistent components such as memory, prompts, skills, and tools. We call this process harness evolution. However, such evolution could introduce unexpected safety risks. Existing work studies harness misevolution and validates candidate harnesses or attributed individual component updates, leaving safety analysis of cross-component update interactions largely unexamined. To address this gap, we study compositional safety failures in harness evolution, where interactions among individually safe and utility-preserving component updates can produce undesirable or unsafe agent behavior, revealing a safety risk intrinsic to harness evolution. Across three safety-related benchmarks, we identify 43 pairwise and 18 irreducible 3-way compositional safety failures. Conventional solution incurs combinatorial complexity in validating cross-component interactions, leaving the safety checking impractical as the harness evolves. To solve this, we introduced a typed hypergraph that represents component states as nodes and safety-relevant higher-order interactions as hyperedges. When the harness changes, the hypergraph updates only the interaction neighborhood of the changed states rather than reconstructing the global composition space. Building on that, we develop a hypergraph-guided runtime monitoring mechanism. Experiments show that our method effectively mitigates compositional safety risks while preserving task utility and reducing interaction-checking costs, and further reveal an empirical safety-utility-cost trade-off across different safety mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Zhixiang Zhang, Zesen Liu, Wai Ip Lai, Hongxu chen, Dongdong She
